analysis.one_liner: Replaces asbestos lawsuits with a no-fault industry-funded compensation fund for sick workers.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee reported the bill favorably in July 2003 and it was placed on the Senate calendar, but it never received a vote before the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have shut down the court system for asbestos cases and replaced it with a national trust fund. Companies that made or used asbestos and their insurers would pay fixed amounts — about $45 billion from defendant companies and $52 billion from insurers — into a fund administered by a new federal office. People with asbestos diseases like mesothelioma and asbestosis would apply directly to the fund and receive a scheduled payment based on how sick they were, without having to prove in court that any company was at fault. In exchange, the fund would become the only way to be compensated for asbestos: no more jury trials, and awards would be fixed amounts rather than whatever a jury decided. The bill also banned manufacturing and selling asbestos-containing products, with a few exemptions.
analysis.who_benefits: People already sick or later sickened by asbestos exposure — mesothelioma, lung cancer, and asbestosis patients, many of them retired industrial and shipyard workers — would get a guaranteed, no-fault payment from a large pooled fund instead of waiting years in court and hoping the company they sue stays solvent. Workers and pensioners at companies being drained by asbestos lawsuits would also benefit from the certainty the cap provides. Companies facing asbestos liability, and their insurers, gain the most concrete benefit: their exposure is capped at fixed contributions and every existing and future asbestos lawsuit is extinguished.

how_it_helps.text: Claimants would not have to prove any company's negligence — eligibility turned only on having a qualifying asbestos disease and sufficient exposure.

Eligible claimants would receive scheduled awards from a fund financed by roughly $97 billion in fixed contributions from defendant companies and insurers, rather than depending on the solvency of any single company being sued.

The bill required expedited handling for claimants with exigent circumstances, covered uninsured medical monitoring (x-rays and lung-function tests every three years), and waived exposure documentation for workers and residents of Libby, Montana, the site of severe asbestos contamination.
It banned the manufacture, processing, and distribution of asbestos-containing products, with narrow exemptions (for example, chlor-alkali diaphragms and fully encapsulated roofing products).
By capping and centralizing liability, the bill's stated aim was to end the wave of asbestos-driven corporate bankruptcies that the bill's own findings said were endangering jobs and pensions.

analysis.who_pays: Defendant companies pay $45 billion and insurers $52 billion into the fund over its life. The other cost falls on victims: they give up the right to sue in court, take fixed scheduled awards paid in installments over roughly three years, have those awards reduced by any other compensation received, and lose out entirely if their claim misses strict medical criteria or a four-year filing deadline.
analysis.who_pays_short: Defendant companies and insurers; victims give up jury trials

drawbacks.text: The fund would have been the exclusive remedy: after it opened, no asbestos claim could be pursued in federal or state court, so victims gave up jury trials and full tort damages in exchange for fixed scheduled awards.

Awards were set by a fixed benefit table, paid in structured installments over three years, and reduced by any collateral-source compensation the claimant had received — victims with strong cases would likely recover less than in court.

Strict medical and exposure requirements — a 10-year latency period, five or more weighted years of substantial occupational exposure (with post-1986 exposure counted at one-tenth value), and specific x-ray and lung-function thresholds — would have excluded claimants who could have won in court, and a four-year filing deadline extinguished missed claims.

Total industry contributions were capped ($45 billion from defendants, $52 billion from insurers), so if claims exceeded projections the fund's adequacy depended on the Administrator extracting additional contributions from the same participants.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For very sick claimants — mesothelioma and severe asbestosis — the trade was appealing: a guaranteed, faster payment from a large pooled fund instead of years of litigation against companies that might go bankrupt first. But the costs were real. Awards were fixed by a benefit table and paid in installments over three years, reduced by other compensation, and cut off if not claimed within four years of diagnosis — so victims with strong cases would likely receive less than a jury might award, and the sickest paid the price of the certainty granted to defendants. Whether the fund was large enough for everyone who qualified was the central open question, and the bill never got far enough for that debate to be settled.

outcome.mechanism: The Judiciary Committee approved and reported the bill in July 2003 and it sat on the Senate calendar, but no floor vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced May 22, 2003 by Senator Hatch and referred to the Judiciary Committee.
The committee held hearings on June 4, 2003 and held three markup sessions in June before ordering the bill reported favorably with amendments on July 10.
The committee reported the bill with amendments on July 30, 2003, with a written report (No. 108-118) to which additional and minority views were filed.

The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 239) on July 30, 2003 — the waiting list for bills awaiting floor consideration — and no further action was taken.
The bill received no floor vote and died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies facing asbestos suits and their insurers kept the status quo — no fixed multibillion-dollar assessments and no end to case-by-case litigation — while sick workers were left with the slow court system the bill was written to replace. The plaintiffs' bar also kept its docket.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Asbestos defendants and insurers; claimants kept the status quo

for.name: Orrin Hatch
for.role: U.S. Senator from Utah, Chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, chaired its hearings and markups, and reported it to the Senate with amendments.

for.name: 2 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Ben Nelson of Nebraska, Zell Miller of Georgia)

against.name: Minority members of the Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Filed minority views against the committee's report of the bill.

against.name: Association of Trial Lawyers of America (now AAJ)
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against asbestos trust-fund legislation, arguing the fund was too small and the medical criteria too strict for many genuinely sick victims.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan in form — Hatch (R) with 5 Republican and 2 Democratic cosponsors — but the committee's minority filed views against the report, and the bill's core sponsors were Republican.

industries.industry: Companies with asbestos liability (manufacturers, builders, and their successors)
industries.note: The bill would have capped their total exposure at $45 billion in scheduled contributions, ended all asbestos lawsuits against them, and let them seek hardship and inequity adjustments to lower their assessments. Their gain came directly at victims' expense: no more jury awards, and claimants with strong cases locked into lower fixed payments.

Insurers would have paid a fixed $52 billion allocation set by a new Asbestos Insurers Commission, replacing open-ended liability on old policies, with several-not-joint liability and a private right of action to squeeze non-paying reinsurers. Certainty at a capped price is worth more than unbounded litigation risk.

Making the fund the exclusive remedy would have eliminated the contingency-fee lawsuit system that handled hundreds of thousands of asbestos claims. The trial bar's loss was part of what the bill's sponsors counted as a feature.

Title V would have banned manufacturing, processing, and distributing asbestos-containing products, with exemptions only where no safe substitute existed, for critical defense and NASA uses, and for chlor-alkali diaphragms and fully encapsulated roofing materials. Here the industry's loss ran alongside the public's interest.
